title: University of Arkansas, D-Wave to partner on quantum computing project
excerpt: D-Wave Quantum Inc., a Palo Alto, Calif.-based quantum computing company, and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas...
content:
D-Wave Quantum Inc., a Palo Alto, Calif.-based quantum computing company, and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas are collaborating to explore quantum computing’s impact on complex supply chain problems.

According to a Monday (Oct. 5) news release, the collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund to advance thought leadership, education, and independent research on applying quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. D-Wave and the UA announced the collaboration Monday at CSCMP EDGE 2026, a four-day conference and exhibition hosted in Nashville, Tenn., by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals.

D-Wave has also joined the Supply Chain Management Research Center’s partnership program, which has more than 25 industry partners. A UA spokeswoman said D-Wave gave $50,000 for the initiative and will receive entitlements from the Supply Chain Management Research Center. Membership is year-to-year, and the gift is project-focused “instead of a cadenced amount.” A UA spokesman said the entitlements provide access to UA events and students.

According to D-Wave, it’s the first commercial supplier of quantum computers and the only one to offer dual-platform quantum computing products and services, spanning annealing and gate-model quantum computing technologies. According to IBM, quantum computing is an emergent field of computer science and engineering that uses quantum mechanics to solve problems faster than classical supercomputers.

The release shows that supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience. Quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are being implemented as networks grow more complex and disruptions become more consequential.

The collaboration between D-Wave and the Supply Chain Management Research Center is expected to explore quantum optimization research for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, and scheduling and decision-making under disruption. The joint effort may also include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, industry engagement, government and academic stakeholders, and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.

“Supply chains are highly dynamic, with decision-making that can have a far-reaching impact on efficiency and costs,” said Murray Thom, vice president of quantum technology evangelism at D-Wave. “We’re seeing quantum computing technologies emerge as potentially powerful alternatives to existing classical approaches. The Walton College is at the forefront of supply chain innovation, not only educating the next generation of supply chain professionals and conducting groundbreaking research but also engaging industry to effect economic change. We’re thrilled to support the college as it facilitates a quantum-ready supply chain.”

“The Walton College is dedicated to exploring the very latest methods, processes and technologies that advance supply chain management and resilience,” said Brian Fugate, associate dean for research and graduate programs at Walton College. “Quantum computing is showing great potential to help organizations accelerate decision-making, mitigate disruption and drive better operational outcomes. We’re excited to partner with D-Wave, one of the quantum computing industry’s foremost leaders, to bring quantum into our research portfolio and ultimately benefit students and partners alike.”
